cards.title: Greedy versus bit-optimal LZ77 over arbitrary alphabets
cards.formal: Determine the worst-case ratio R(n,z,σ) between greedy and bit-optimal classical LZ77 encodings, up to universal constant factors jointly in n,z,σ. Let S(n,z,σ) be the strings s∈{0,1,…,n}ⁿ with exactly σ distinct symbols and exactly z phrases in the greedy parsing defined below. The domain D consists of all integer triples n≥2, 2≤σ≤z≤n for which S(n,z,σ) is nonempty. Define R(n,z,σ)=max_{s∈S(n,z,σ)} G(s)/B(s), where G is the least bit cost among references realizing the greedy parsing and B is the least bit cost among all valid parsings and their references. Give a positive function g on D and constants a,A>0,N independent of all three parameters such that a g(n,z,σ)≤R(n,z,σ)≤A g(n,z,σ) for every (n,z,σ)∈D with n≥N. The target is the complete joint tradeoff, including growing alphabets and highly repetitive strings.
cards.why: Tests how far the central greedy choice in dictionary compression can depart from the best bit representation, and how text length, repetitiveness and alphabet size jointly control that loss. A full tradeoff would distinguish intrinsic limitations of greedy parsing from costs that occur only in special input regimes.

sentences: Greedy LZ77 minimizes the number of phrases, but variable-length codes can make another parsing shorter in bits.
This question asks for the largest greedy-to-optimal bit-cost ratio jointly in text length n, greedy phrase count z and alphabet size σ.
The model uses classical overlapping copy-plus-literal triples with fixed logarithmic integer codes.
Known bounds settle constant alphabets and the ratio maximized over all phrase counts, but leave the full three-parameter tradeoff open.
The extremal domain uses exact feasible phrase counts; existing lower-bound constructions reported with Θ(z) phrases are not silently treated as exact-count results.

cards.definitions:
Positions in s are numbered 1,…,n. A parsing partitions s into nonempty consecutive phrases. A phrase of length ℓ starting at p is valid if ℓ=1, or if some integer j with 1≤j

1; set d=0 when ℓ=1. Thus the source offset is one less than the usual distance p−j, and a copied phrase can have d=0. Every phrase retains its last symbol as a literal, including the final phrase. The greedy parsing chooses the longest valid phrase at every successive start position; this fixes phrase boundaries, not the earlier reference. For each nonnegative integer x use the Elias gamma code of x+1: write its binary representation of length b and prepend b−1 zero bits. Its length is L(x)=2⌊log₂(x+1)⌋+1. The cost of a triple is L(d)+L(ℓ)+L(c), and the encoding cost is the sum over phrases, in bits. No alphabet dictionary, external header, sliding window or entropy coding is charged or supplied. Alphabet labels themselves are the integers in the input; a free renaming to {0,…,σ−1} is not allowed. G minimizes this cost over every legal reference for the fixed greedy boundaries; B minimizes over all valid parsings and references. Both minima are over nonempty finite sets, and B>0. The maximum defining R is therefore attained on D. This fixed code makes the quantity unambiguous. At constant-factor precision it represents the source’s fixed encoders for d,ℓ,c whose positive-integer code lengths are Θ(log₂(x+1)), with bounded fixed costs for zero and positive cost for each positive length. Triple costs, and hence each optimum and their ratio, differ by bounded factors under any such fixed encoders; those comparison constants may depend on the encoders, never on n,z,σ. The source’s Θ bound is understood for all positive integers, not as permission for a zero-cost positive phrase length. There is no running-time or randomness requirement on computing a parsing in this extremal question. Matching lower bounds must concern valid strings in the specified parameter class, not merely a poor reference choice for a greedy parsing.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish matching constant-factor upper and lower bounds for R throughout D as specified. Describe the asymptotic dependence rather than merely restating the defining finite maximization. A lower bound for a family with Θ(z) phrases must state its actual phrase counts; it is not automatically a lower bound for every feasible triple with exactly z phrases. A bound depending only on n, a constant-alphabet result, or an improvement in one regime is partial progress unless the full joint domain is covered.

context_blocks.title: Fewest phrases need not mean fewest bits
context_blocks.text: The greedy parsing minimizes the number of phrases, but long references and literal codes have variable bit costs. The paper analyzes the loss relative to the best parsing under fixed logarithmic integer encoders, rather than relative to an unrestricted compressor.

context_blocks.title: Known bounds leave an alphabet-dependent gap
context_blocks.text: Theorem 7 gives the upper bound O(min{z, log₂ n / log₂(log_σ z)}). Theorem 10 constructs length-n strings with σ symbols and Θ(z) greedy phrases attaining Ω(min{z, log₂ n /(log₂(log_σ z)+log₂ σ)}), for its stated range σ≤z≤n/log_σ n. For interpreting these asymptotic expressions at small arguments, logarithmic denominator terms can be bounded below by 1; the positive constant cost per phrase supplies the corresponding coarse bound. These displays do not assert a construction with every exact feasible phrase count.

context_blocks.title: Several maximized or restricted cases are settled
context_blocks.text: For constant alphabets the paper matches the bounds in the usual parameter-scale sense. Maximizing over phrase counts gives Θ(log n / log log log n) in the constant-alphabet case, whereas allowing arbitrary alphabets gives Θ(log n). Theorem 12 already attains the latter loss with O(log n) symbols and O(log² n) greedy phrases. These n-only results do not determine the whole three-parameter tradeoff.

context_blocks.title: Precise quantitative interpretation
context_blocks.text: The concluding question asks for tight bounds in n,z,σ. This card makes the underlying extremal ratio explicit, using exact feasible parameter triples and one representative encoder. This exact-parameter convention is stronger than merely exhibiting lower-bound families whose phrase counts are controlled within constant factors; the source’s existing lower bounds are recorded with that limitation.

context_blocks.title: Other LZ77 comparisons use different costs
context_blocks.text: The later comparison of LZ77 variants bounds the numbers of greedy phrases when overlap and phrase syntax change. It does not supply matching bounds on the bit-cost ratio between greedy and optimal parsings in this card.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
